title: Peter and Paul in Rome (c. 64–67)
hook: tradition holds Peter was crucified upside down and Paul beheaded under Nero

segments.voice: Yesterday, year three opened with Acts stopping in a rented room in Rome. Your line was saints and sinners, both. Did you catch the other half of a story? Day six hundred ninety-eight.

By the Sea of Tiberias, after a breakfast of bread and fish, the risen Jesus tells Peter how his life will end. When you were younger, he says, you dressed yourself and walked where you liked. When you are old, you will stretch out your hands, and another will dress you and lead you where you would not go. John adds one quiet line: Jesus said this to show by what death Peter would glorify God. Then the Bible goes silent on it. Where Peter's road ends, and Paul's, is told by the generations after.
screen: `BY THE SEA OF TIBERIAS.` → `YOU WILL STRETCH OUT YOUR HANDS.` → `THE BIBLE GOES SILENT.`

segments.voice: Start with Paul. In the Second Letter to Timothy, Paul writes as a prisoner to a younger friend, in the Douay-Rheims: "I have fought a good fight, I have finished my course, I have kept the faith." A few lines later he asks Timothy to hurry and come before winter, and to bring the cloak he left behind, and his books. That's the voice of a man who knows the end is close. Now the tradition. Early Christian writers, collected by the historian Eusebius, say both apostles died in Rome under the emperor Nero. Tradition says Paul, who Acts tells us was a Roman citizen, was beheaded. And tradition says Peter was crucified, and asked to hang head downward, because he did not think himself worthy to die the way his Lord had. That detail comes from writings outside the Bible; Catholics hold it as tradition, not scripture. Now the carry. The rock: in Matthew's Gospel Jesus gives Simon a new name, "thou art Peter; and upon this rock I will build my church." Catholics see the bishops of Rome as Peter's successors, and Saint Peter's Basilica stands over the place tradition names as his grave. The tentmaker: Acts says Paul worked with his hands making tents, and Paul writes that he labored night and day so as not to be a burden. A fisherman and a craftsman, and not always at peace: Paul says he opposed Peter to his face in Antioch over who could eat with whom. And yet the Church keeps their feast together, on one day. Some paintings and statues set them side by side, Peter holding the keys, Paul holding the sword that tradition says took his head. A fisherman and a craftsman, and between them a quarrel that neither the Bible nor the Church ever hid.
screen: `I HAVE KEPT THE FAITH.` · `ROME, UNDER NERO: TRADITION.` · `THE ROCK AND THE TENTMAKER.` · `TWO WHO ARGUED, ONE FEAST.` · then, large: `UPON THIS ROCK I WILL BUILD MY CHURCH.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: remember Christians who suffer for their faith today. Settle, and breathe. You don't need names or places. Think of someone, somewhere, who will go to Mass this week knowing it could cost them: a job, a home, their safety. Hold them for a moment the way you'd hold a friend's hand in a waiting room. If you pray, you can ask for their courage and their protection, and for the people who threaten them, too. If you don't pray, simply keep them in mind while the minutes pass. The bell holds the time.
Cephas. The Aramaic name John also gives Simon Peter, alongside the Greek Petros, rock. Today's word.
Your line: the rock and the tentmaker. Today, think of someone you disagree with who works for the same good you do, and say one kind word about them. Day six hundred ninety-eight.

howItsDone: Catholics keep one shared feast for Saints Peter and Paul, pray at the tombs tradition names as theirs in Rome, and pray for persecuted Christians at Mass and in their own prayers.

original.note: Greek: Peter — in Matthew 16:18 the name sits beside petra, rock. John gives the Aramaic too: Cephas.

trapdoor: what you thought: the Bible ends with Peter and Paul martyred in Rome.
what it means: the Bible stops before their deaths. the Rome story is the Church's tradition.
what a scholar hears: Eusebius gathering earlier writers on how and where the two apostles died, and the Acts of Peter giving the cross upside down.

notes: 2 Timothy 4:7 and Matthew 16:18 Douay-Rheims (Challoner) wording: confirm exact text.
Script attributes the Nero-era deaths in Rome to tradition via Eusebius (HE 2.25 citing Gaius and Dionysius of Corinth; HE 3.1 citing Origen for Peter crucified head downward). Confirm references.

Peter's reason (unworthy to die as the Lord did) follows the Acts of Peter and later tradition (e.g. Jerome); Origen via Eusebius gives head downward without that reason in some readings. Confirm attribution.
Pauline authorship of 2 Timothy is debated by some scholars; script calls it 'the second letter to Timothy' and does not argue the point.
Title date 'c. 64–67' is the index's; script states no date in the voice.
Shared feast of Peter and Paul (29 June) mentioned without date.

Audit: the teach ended by saying the Church keeps them together twice in a row; the close now ends on the keys, the sword and the quarrel nobody hid. The sword as the instrument of Paul's death is iconographic tradition: confirm.

Editor: 'beach in Galilee' now 'by the Sea of Tiberias' as John 21:1 names it; Paul's 'own words' softened to 'Paul writes' (2 Timothy authorship debated); 'so different that' causal link removed from the Antioch quarrel; 'In Catholic art they often stand' cut to 'some paintings and statues'; garbled 'would not tell their stories apart' fixed; added John 21:9–13, Jerome (the unworthy reason) and the calendar feast as sources.
